FBA often says we’re cosplaying them but FBA isn’t all African Americans. A lot of this noise comes from non-Black agents online spreading confusion. It’s a small group using culture to deny African and Caribbean roots. This isn’t imitation, it’s shared heritage. Let’s break it down.

FBA says, “Stop cosplaying us with gold teeth,”
But gold teeth go way back. Ancient Egyptians used them to show wealth. The Aeta people in the Philippines wore them for beauty. Across Africa and Asia, gold teeth were a symbol of status long before grills hit the U.S.

FBA says, “Stop cosplaying us with weaves and locs,”
Weaves started in Ancient Egypt (3400 B.C.) using human hair, wool, and plant fibers for royalty. The Yoruba and Zulu used hair for ceremony and social rank. The Himba mold their locs in red clay. Maasai warriors grow red locs, and in Ghana, locs tied into spiritual identity. Even Hindu sadhus and ancient Nazarites had locs before Rastafari.

FBA says, “Stop cosplaying us with braids,”
Braids were cultural codes across Africa. Fulani women used beads and cowries. Yoruba created shuku styles. The Himba mixed clay and butter into their braids. Wolof women braided cornrows as maps of heritage. Zulu braids marked age and status.

FBA says, “Stop cosplaying us with nose rings and earrings,”
Berber and Beja women wore nose rings for status and marriage. Dinka and Nuer men wore large earrings to show age. The Maasai stretched their ears to show strength and beauty. These traditions had meaning far beyond decoration.

FBA says, “Stop cosplaying us with tattoos,” 
But tattoos go back to 2000 B.C. in Egypt used by women for fertility and protection. In Ethiopia and Berber culture, tattoos warded off evil and showed tribal ties. Nubians tattooed symbols of goddesses and spiritual power.

FBA says, “Y’all copying us wearing gold chains,” 
But Africans made gold fashion centuries ago. The Akan of Ghana wore “Sika Futuro” thick gold chains for royalty. Fulani and Tuareg women wore bold gold jewelry for honor. Hip-hop revived that legacy, it didn’t invent it.

FBA says, “Y’all copying us wearing jeans,”
But stars like Sidney Poitier, Harry Belafonte, and Grace Jones Caribbean legends wore jeans before they were trendy. Back then, jeans were for laborers, not fashion. The Caribbean made it cool before it hit hip-hop.

FBA says, “Y’all copying our BBQ culture,”
But barbecue comes from Haiti and Taíno land. The word “barbacoa” is Taíno. Africans brought the flavor, technique, and slow-smoking genius that evolved into Southern BBQ. It didn’t start in Texas it started in resistance.

FBA says, “Y’all copying our soul food,”
But ingredients like okra and black-eyed peas came from Africa. Callaloo still used in Caribbean dishes is native to West Africa too. Much of what’s now “soul food” started as African survival food in the Americas.

FBA says, “We invented rap,”
Yes and no. Modern hip-hop was shaped by real African Americans (not FBA coons) but the roots go deeper. Fela Kuti’s “Roforofo Fight” (1972) featured rhythmic bars over live beats with political fire matching the definition of rap. Africans were spitting truth on beats long before the Bronx. Fela didn’t just create Afrobeat he laid the groundwork for conscious rap.
